It’s Selfish, It’s Hokey, and I’ll Lose My Edge: 3 Half-Truths About Self-Compassion

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (605 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m a late adopter of a lot of things.
  • Why such reluctance to embrace the research-backed practice of self-compassion?
  • According to recent reports, we think that being kind to ourselves is self-indulgent and self-focused.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m a late adopter of a lot of things. It took me two years to get an iPhone, a lot of convincing to wear AirPods (which I still call ear pods despite my son’s cringe), and it took me even longer to drink the “self-compassion” Kool-Aid. (Which I guess I drank because I wrote a book on how to practice self-compassion daily!).

Why such reluctance to embrace the research-backed practice of self-compassion? I believed three things about self-compassion that turned me off. But I’ve since learned, they are really only half-truths.

According to recent reports, we think that being kind to ourselves is self-indulgent and self-focused. Yet the research shows that when you practice self-compassion, you are more likely to:.

If you are a parent, you probably know this firsthand. When you practice caring for yourself, you are less likely to have your stress spill over onto your kids. But there is a half-truth to self-compassion making you selfish.

In other words, if you are worried that self-compassion will make you selfish, focus more on how giving yourself compassion will help you be of service to others. One body-based practice I like to do with this concept is a simple breathing exercise:.

Breathing in, I take in care and understanding.Breathing out, I send out care and understanding.

There is a large body of research showing that self-compassion actually helps you perform better, not worse.

According to recent reports, self-compassion helps you stay on track with your wisest values and goals. The half-truth? When you practice self-compassion you may choose to lose your edge a little…in good ways.

As you learn to listen more to your body and stop berating yourself for mistakes, you naturally may want to give up on pushing yourself in ways that are harmful. I’ve lost my edge when it comes to having to run every day, getting every email returned in a timely manner, and making the perfect dinner for my family (hello Trader Joe’s frozen aisle!) … and that’s a good thing.

It has been revealed that when my clients are struggling with whether or not they should push themselves at something, I ask them to do what contemplative leader Stephen Batchelor suggested to me: Drop the question into your belly. If you struggle with self-criticism or rigid rules, your belly is likely to have a more compassionate answer than your head!

Industry observers note that it can feel uncomfortable to say nice things to yourself, and sometimes downright cheesy. I rarely recommend clients cheer themselves on with the “Good job” or “Way to go!” statements that some motivational coaches suggest.

Industry observers note that self-compassion is relating to yourself in a way that is encouraging, warm, realistic, and just right for you. You don’t need to recite a list of loving-kindness mantras or put your hand on your heart if you find those practices hokey. Sometimes self-compassion is as simple as noticing the part of you that is scared and being with it a little longer.

The half-truth? When you practice self-compassion, you just might start to adopt some hokey platitudes toward yourself. But hey, they are platitudes for a good reason, right?

To learn more about how to bring self-compassion into your daily life, read The Self-Compassion Daily Journal by Dr. Diana Hill or listen to the Wise Effort Podcast.

It has been revealed that diana Hill, PhD is a clinical psychologist, international trainer and sought-out speaker on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and compassion. Host of the Wise Effort podcast, author of The Self-Compassion Daily Journal, and co-author the ACT Daily Journal. @drdianahill.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an Australian first, WHEN provides at-home egg count testing and access to the country’s leading fertility experts — prompting a conversation about how and when people can access their own fertility information.
  • The conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown.
  • Traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an Australian first, WHEN provides at-home egg count testing and access to the country’s leading fertility experts — prompting a conversation about how and when people can access their own fertility information. They came to us to conceive a brand that could balance credibility and compassion in equal measure. One that felt just as comfortable in a trusted doctor’s office as the shiny shelves of a global beauty store.

The conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown. But with all that focus on the fear-inducing countdown, there’s not a lot of helpful talk — about how fertility works, the proactive steps we can take to improve it, or why the biological clock is an outdated trope. That’s where WHEN comes in — a fertility medtech manufacturer on a mission to ensure no one with ovaries is left wondering about them.

Traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise. But this narrow focus has resulted in a category that feels overly clinical and sometimes cold, losing sight of the real people at the heart of it all. We saw an opportunity to create something that balanced the two — trust and credibility, with warmth and humanity. A direct-to-consumer lifestyle brand built on deep medical experience that felt equally at home in a retail environment.

Industry observers note that fertility is, understandably, incredibly personal and seldom discussed. To get to the heart of the issue, our friends at VML conducted a series of focus groups, one-on-one interviews and stakeholder research. Because in failing to talk about it, we’re failing to give people the information they need at the right time. People are proactive about pap smears, mammograms, skin checks, sexual health tests—all considered lead indicators that look ahead to impact the future. But fertility is measured as a lag indicator, only measured once it’s more difficult to affect the outcome.

Without jumping through costly medical hoops, there is no accessible way for people to know what’s happening inside their very own bodies without a referral. The medical industry is not set up to provide this kind of information proactively, which can make people feel blocked. And when it comes to fertility, information is power.

Industry observers note that given WHEN is the first of its kind in Australia, care needed to be taken to communicate the importance and impact of its service. Credible medical expertise was a leading reason to believe. But we also knew people needed to hear the real stories behind the brand to build trust in something so upcoming. Striking the balance was critical.

It has been revealed that the result is a visual and verbal system that blends emotion with science, expression with information. Designed to showcase fertility stories, expert advice and the endless questions we ask ourselves, the brand moves seamlessly from packaging to print, retail stores to social media.

Industry observers note that the WHEN wordmark sits at the heart of the visual identity. Clear and confident, it anchors the brand as a dependable figure in the health and medical space. Paired with an organic cell shape that reacts to the world around it, the wordmark and logoform are a perfect foil to the other. Together, they represent standing strong amid the ever-changing nature of life.

WHEN’s typeface is ABC Diatype. It’s used for everything — from wordmark to body copy. Chosen for its modernity and scientific edge, it brings calm and clarity to everything we say. Paired with a colour palette of lemon and neutrals, the identity feels light and warm against an industry so often cold and clinical.

An key first touchpoint was the at-home testing kit — the Egg Count Check. The kit is split into three sections: Prepare, Collect, and Send. We designed the packaging experience to follow the same logical structure, ensuring the steps were simple to follow and easy to use.

Inspired by the sleek aesthetic of our favourite tech brands, the kit’s box takes a rigid form with special attention paid to premium print finishes. We also created a custom instruction booklet to guide the user through the process, designed and illustrated in-house.

Industry observers note that our primary photography style uses intimate portraits and close crops to focus on the subject’s internal thoughts and feelings. We aim to capture moments that feel like a natural extension of everyday life, empowering and relatable in their familiarity. As a secondary style, we splice natural textures and fluid forms with our portraits, like fragments of memory telling the story of a person’s inner world.

Industry observers note that to further enhance this sense of intimacy, a series of icons were developed to capture the different states of mind one might feel around this sensitive and personal topic. Following the same visual language as the logo, these icons add flexibility and expression to the brand, especially when used with the intimate portraiture.

The brand name itself is a question — when? But it’s also a statement of intent. We worked with copywriter Amy Scott to develop a verbal concept exploring the idea of an inner monologue, giving voice to the questions we ask ourselves but perhaps never verbalise. The brand speaks as an empathetic expert, both insightful and inclusive. By creating space for open conversation and asking the questions people ask themselves, we show no matter where they’re at in their fertility journey, they’re not alone.

WHEN doesn’t only set to change fertility testing, but to also facilitate an aspirational platform that aims to drive community and empowering conversation around fertility. The brand was crafted to grow into a multidimensional platform for fertility information access and support. We helped design the first step of this journey through WHEN Matters — a curated blog for sharing real fertility stories and credible medical expertise to ensure no one with ovaries was left feeling alone on their journey.

We behave rather well in grocery stores, wouldn’t you say?

There we all are, from different backgrounds, in different modes of dress, shopping for different dietary preferences, moving along at different speeds, some clutching baskets, others pushing carts, wending in and out of aisles and finally assuming our place in the checkout line without crashing into each other. Sometimes our behavior is exemplary, like when some poor soul accidentally sets off an avalanche of oranges by extracting the exact wrong one from the mountainous display, and one or two of us scramble into action, scooping them up and cheerfully placing them back in formation. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • AltaMed Health Services, a major healthcare provider in Southern California, is opening an art gallery, library and cultural centre to house its art collection in the Los Angeles suburb of Montebello.
  • AltaMed began collecting art in the 1970s, based on a belief that art is an integral part of holistic well-being.
  • Industry observers note that “Our collection focuses on Chicano art," Cástulo de la Rocha, the president and chief executive of AltaMed (and founder of the collection), stated in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AltaMed Health Services, a major healthcare provider in Southern California, is opening an art gallery, library and cultural centre to house its art collection in the Los Angeles suburb of Montebello. AltaMed’s collection, more than 50 years in the making, includes works by Laura Aguilar, Graciela Iturbide, Gabriel Orozco and others. Its upcoming 30,000-sq.-ft space, The Alta, opens to the public on Sunday (15 November).

AltaMed began collecting art in the 1970s, based on a belief that art is an integral part of holistic well-being. Since then, its collection has grown to some 4,000 pieces, with about 1,400 of them right now placed in its offices and clinics.

Industry observers note that “Our collection focuses on Chicano art," Cástulo de la Rocha, the president and chief executive of AltaMed (and founder of the collection), stated in a statement. "Because AltaMed was founded as part of the Chicano Movement in the 1970s, because I was active in the Chicano Movement, and because our patients and employees can connect culturally with the art.”.

Sources indicate that in recent years, AltaMed has been converting a warehouse on the edge of a shopping mall in Montebello to house its collection. The space will have regular hours for visitors to tour its gallery, see works on shelves and sliding racks in open storage, and watch behind-the-scenes processes of digitisation and conservation. There is also studio space for artist residencies on site.

Patssi Valdez and rafa esparza’s Sacred and Profane Beauty (2026) Courtesy AltaMed.

“The collection is here to serve the communities that AltaMed is focused on in Los Angeles and Orange County, primarily Latino communities,” Pilar Tompkins Rivas, AltaMed’s chief curator and vice president of arts, tells The Art Newspaper. “So we think about art that is relevant and celebratory of those populations.”.

Sources indicate that some recently acquired and commissioned works also address health and community—such as Sonia Romero’s mural The Fence-Pomona (2026), made expressly for the central communal space in a senior-care facility in nearby Pomona. The mural is 6ft high and 10ft wide, depicting a white lattice fence festooned with roses and the San Gabriel Mountains behind it. It ioverlooks a space used for meals, artmaking and gathering for patients.

AltaMed’s collection runs the gamut of media and spans more than 100 years, although most of the work was made after the Second World War. Early pieces include those of Hernando Gonzallo Villa, a commercial artist who famously designed ads and posters for the Santa Fe Railway. More recent works include drawings, prints and paintings by Carlos Almaraz, Judy Baca, Camille Rose Garcia, Gronk, Frank Romero, Eloy Torrez, John Valadez and Linda Vallejo.

The artist Felicia Montes at La Botánica del Barrio (2026) Courtesy AltaMed.

Sources indicate that the first exhibition in the gallery is Patssi Valdez: LA LA LA (until 9 April 2027), featuring photo-based and collage works by a pioneer of Los Angeles’s Chicano art movement. For this show, Valdez re-created some of her photography from the 1970s and 80s—portraits of friends that helped define punk and goth glamour.

Sources indicate that she indicates she had discussed doing something “out of the box” with AltaMed, and several of the framed work have coloured strips of paper flying out from the frame. To highlight some of her portraits, Valdez added Swarovski crystals to the prints, such as in Divine Dede (2026) and Hot Pink (Mario, Charlie & DeDe) (1983/2025). She also co-created work in collaboration with two younger artists, rafa esparza and Gabriela Ruiz.

Industry observers note that it has been more than a decade since Valdez had a solo exhibition. “AltaMed has been a collector of my work for quite a while and has been very supportive," she claims. The company has purchased Valdez’s paintings and photography, and even one of her signature full-size paper dresses. One of these dresses is in a glass case in The Alta’s open-storage area.

Sources indicate that down the hall are the residency studios. The artist Rubén Esparza is working in one of them, where he has been making multimedia pieces featuring his "ongoing exploration of the cultural significance of Latinx, Chicano and Queer diasporas".

Sources indicate that the other studio has been transformed into an educational apothecary by Felicia Montes and her collective Mujeres de Maíz. La Botánica del Barrio (2026) features displays of samplable traditional herbal teas and tinctures, as well as a decorated pushcart. In the hallway, The Wellness Wall lets visitors put up cards with their own home remedies and healing practices. Visitors have suggested some very practical cures—from "talk to friends" and "travelling" to "Vicks" and "a good mezcal".

What Science Reveals About Gratitude’s Impact on the Brain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that gratitude is celebrated throughout philosophy and religion; recent scientific studies suggest it carries significant benefits for our mental and physical health.
  • Because better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits and help people understand the importance of fostering this powerful emotion.
  • Better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gratitude is celebrated throughout philosophy and religion; recent scientific studies suggest it carries significant benefits for our mental and physical health. But very little is known about what actually happens in our brain and body when we experience it.

Why does that matter? Because better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits and help people understand the importance of fostering this powerful emotion. The goal of my research has been to lay the groundwork for understanding what happens in the brain when we feel grateful—and a picture of the grateful brain is now starting to emerge.

Better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits.

When I first embarked on the journey to study gratitude, I came across philosophical treatises and religious exhortations emphasizing the importance of gratitude, along with scientific studies suggesting that gratitude can improve your sleep, enhance your romantic relationships, protect you from illness, motivate you to exercise, and boost your happiness, among many other benefits.

At the time, however, very little was known about what happens in our brains and bodies when we experience gratitude, which made it difficult to understand how gratitude actually works. Since I’m a neuroscientist, I zeroed in on the neurobiology of gratitude with a more specific question in mind: Can our brain activity reveal anything about how gratitude achieves its significant benefits?

Given the clear relationship between mental and physical health, I thought that understanding what happens in the brain when we feel gratitude could tell us more about the mind-body connection—namely, how feeling positive emotion can improve bodily functions. I also thought these results could help scientists design programs aimed at generating gratitude by helping them zero in on the precise activities and experiences most essential to reaping gratitude’s benefits.

It has been revealed that it must be said that actually capturing people in the moment of feeling gratitude poses some challenges. After all, some people may not feel gratitude when we expect them to, and others may even feel grateful in unexpected situations. I thought my best bet would be to try to induce gratitude through powerful stories of aid and sacrifice.

According to recent reports, to achieve this, I turned to the USC Shoah Foundation Institute for Visual History, which houses the world’s largest repository of videotaped Holocaust survivor testimonies—many of which, perhaps surprisingly, are filled with breathtaking acts of selflessness and generosity. Along with a team of amazing undergraduates, I began by watching hundreds of hours of survivor testimony to find stories in which the survivor received help of some kind from another person.

According to recent reports, we assembled a collection of these stories and transformed them into short scenarios that we shared with our participants. Each scenario was re-phrased into the second-person (e.g., “You are on a wintertime death march and a fellow prisoner gives you a warm coat”) and presented to our study’s participants. We asked them to imagine themselves in the scenario and feel, as much as possible, how they would feel if they were in the same situation. While participants reflected on these gifts, we measured their brain activity using modern brain imaging techniques (in the form of functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI).

The regions associated with gratitude are part of the neural networks that light up when we socialize and experience pleasure.

For each of these scenarios, we asked participants how much gratitude they felt, and we correlated this rating with their brain activity in that moment. While such an approach will not elicit exactly the same feelings as actually living through such situations, participants overwhelmingly reported strong feelings of gratitude, deep engagement in the task, and, perhaps even more importantly, an increased empathy for and understanding of the Holocaust as a result of participating in the study.

What’s more, our results revealed that when participants reported those grateful feelings, their brains showed activity in a set of regions located in the medial pre-frontal cortex, an area in the frontal lobes of the brain where the two hemispheres meet. This area of the brain is associated with understanding other people’s perspectives, empathy, and feelings of relief. This is also an area of the brain that is massively connected to the systems in the body and brain that regulate emotion and support the process of stress relief.

These data told us a reasonable story about gratitude:.

Glenn Fox, PhD, is a research fellow at USC’s Brain and Creativity Institute. He earned his PhD from the Neuroscience Graduate Program at the University of Southern California working with Antonio Damasio. His research focuses on social cognition, affective neuroscience and social influence.

It has been revealed that here is the core concept. Simple interest earns a return only on your original deposit. If you invest $10,000 at 7% simple interest, you earn $700 per year — every year, forever, on the same $10,000 base. After 30 years, you would have $31,000.

It has been revealed that compound interest earns a return on your original deposit plus all the interest previously earned. In Year 1, you earn $700 on your $10,000. In Year 2, you earn 7% on $10,700 — that is $749. In Year 3, you earn 7% on $11,449 — that is $801. Each year, your interest earns its own interest, and the growth accelerates.

After 30 years of compound interest at 7%, your $10,000 grows to approximately $76,123 — more than double the $31,000 from simple interest. And that is with a single $10,000 deposit and no additional contributions.

The difference starts small and then explodes. In the first 10 years, compound interest adds only $2,672 more than simple interest. In the last 10 years (year 20 to 30), it adds over $30,000 more. This accelerating curve is why time in the market matters more than almost any other factor in building wealth.

After 10 years: $86,500. After 20 years: $260,500. After 30 years: $567,000. You contribute $180,000 of your own money over 30 years. Compound interest adds $387,000 — more than double your contributions. Time is the multiplier that no amount of additional savings can replace.

Paris Photo’s digital sector offers ‘soft photography’ and vital context

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks after an abbreviated edition of Art Basel Paris, the 29th edition of Paris Photo has taken over the Grand Palais (until 15 November), where digital art is enjoying a moment in the spotlight.

Industry observers note that the world of fine art photography is no stranger to controversies involving digital art, and it is heartening to witness the leading photography fair’s commitment to technological excursions within the medium. Featuring 12 exhibitors this year, the fourth iteration of Paris Photo’s digital sector has been curated by Marco De Mutiis of the Fotomuseum Winterthur, taking over from Nina Roehrs, who had helmed the first three editions.

According to recent reports, this year, the digital sector is accompanied by a pedagogical exhibition programme titled Soft Photography, organised by the École Cantonale d'Art de Lausanne in Switzerland and devoted to contextualising the place of AI and CGI within photography. Spanning an interactive exhibition and talks, Soft Photography aims to offer some much-needed dialogue between the medium’s analogue and digital wings.

Paris Photo 2026 at the Grand Palais in Paris © Grégoire Grange.

It has been revealed that the digital sector certainly contains some AI-generated imagery, such as Fresh York- based Heft Gallery’s presentation of Alkan Avcıoğlu’s Disreality series, which is an expansion of the surreal landscape aesthetic he first introduced in a collaboration with Edward Burtynsky. But there are also plenty of analogue images throughout the sector, even photograms, enough to make one wonder just how much of a separate section this really is. A similar dynamic played out in the Zero 10 sector of Art Basel’s Swiss fair last June, where the term “digital art” was used so broadly that it begged the question whether a separate area was really warranted.

Noteworthy presentations at Paris Photo include the Venezuelan gallery Carmen Araujo Arte, which is showcasing Alejandro Cartagena’s mosaic-cut collages. Created from found photographs, the series is a manual interpretation of how images are made by generative AI by gathering found pixels. The works ask timely questions about authorship while also, in a rather sweet, analog gesture, highlighting just how much our art-making inevitably differs from that of algorithmic processes. The results are genuinely magnetic and intimate.

Palo Gallery’s installation of works from the artist duo Adrea Orejarena and Caleb Stein’s American Glitch series interrogates simulation theory as well as the nature of our screen-filled reality. Oscillating somewhere between the tone of David Lynch’s series Twin Peaks and surveillance footage, the presentation is a highlight, particularly Glitch Typologies (2020-24), the seven-channel sequence of floating images projected on the walls of a 3m-by-3m glass cube, the projectors hanging on a rod at its core, reminiscent of CCTV cameras. At a time of growing cultural cynicism, Orejarena and Stein offer a welcome reminder that the intersection of photography and technology can be whimsical, conspiratorial and surprising.

Yumo Wu, Old Dream No.1, 2026 Courtesy the artist and Licheng Ling Projects.

Yumo Wu’s solo stand with Licheng Ling Projects spans AI and darkroom analogue manipulation, with the images interspersed in such a manner that technique—though it inspires a certain sense of wonder—becomes secondary to the impact of the image. It is perhaps the best example at the fair of a presentation that moves beyond our fixation with what might be real and how it may have been created, with the artist instead asking her audience to quietly behold the images’ abstract textures. Wu is an emerging artist whose skill and willingness to experiment drowns out the noise, and the results are rather wonderful to behold. In addition to the stand marking her first solo presentation in Europe, one of her images is included in Paris Photo’s selection marking the bicentennial of the invention of photography.

Vincent Fournier, Orchis nubigena [Kunminga Gemina], 2026 Courtesy of the artist and Au Cube.

Vincent Fournier’s Flora Incognita, presented by Au Cube, features large-scale portraits of speculative flowers derived from existing flora and manipulated to depict what may happen to them on another planet, exposed to different kinds of radiation or gravity. The photos may at first register as AI-generated images, but were in fact created with CGI using Houdini, a comparatively old-school software. Each image is presented in a wooden frame with a golden plaque on the bottom featuring the name of the plant, evoking the kind of 18th- or 19th-century botanical illustration that particularly benefits from the aesthetics of the Grand Palais, whose architecture harks back to a time of earnest scientific fascination and discovery.

Recent findings suggest that the Fresh York gallery Nguyen-Wahed’s solo stand devoted to the Los Angeles-based photographer Summer Wagner contains unframed, romantic, large-scale photographs featuring grainy, densely-textured and coolly-lit portraits. The presentation, only digital insofar as the images were shot on a digital camera, deals with our relationship with reality as "we’ve collectively succumbed to the tsunami or cultural and technological changes that have thrown image-making into an existential crisis”, according to the artist.

Summer Wagner, Blue Shift, 2024 Courtesy of Nguyen Wahed and the artist.

In a recent development, meanwhile, facing the digital sector is Ruttkowski 68’s solo stand devoted to François Hallard’s large-scale Polaroid prints of flowers, with the title “Conversations avec Claude” written by the artist in bold letters at the top of the booth. On the second day of previews, Hallard added “(Monet) not IA” to the title, after countless visitors had presumed the works were related to AI. Evidently Anthropic’s AI engine has eclipsed one of the most consequential painters of the 20th century—at least in its claim to the first name Claude.

Given how much of an impact the nascent field of AI-generated photography has had on photography at large, it is unsurprising that we continue to add disclaimers and coin terms to differentiate the medium’s analogue lineage from its technological step-cousins. Several years ago, the dealer Howard Greenberg told me he favours the term “lens-based” to differentiate the two, and this seemed adequate at the time. But since then, plenty of artists (myself included) have incorporated photographic lenses, enlargers and other analogue tools and processes to experiment with and human-wash digital imagery, so “lens-based” may no longer be up to the task of distinguishing between an image taken with a camera and an image generated with a computer. “Synthetic photography” does have a nice ring to it, although the word itself makes one think of things like latex and carcinogenic sunscreen. Perhaps “soft photography” is the best term, for the moment.

Paris Photo’s digital sector and the Soft Photography programming deftly and quietly tackle the discipline’s ongoing existential crisis by demonstrating that digital art predates many of the technologies we are debating today, and its applications in contemporary photography today are legion.

According to recent reports, the objects we carry often reveal more about us than we realize. From the jewelry we wear to the accessories we keep within reach, even the smallest possessions become expressions of personal style. Yet as technology plays an increasingly central role in our lives, the devices we interact with most remain largely defined by their utility. Bringing more personality to these everyday essentials is the idea behind Pocket Full of Joy—a new collaboration between ESR, a consumer tech accessories brand, and creative duo Craig & Karl—which transforms phone cases and wallets into colorful, functional accessories.

According to recent reports, known for their vibrant compositions and playful iconography, Craig & Karl bring their distinctive visual language to a collection of iPhone cases and magnetic wallets. The collaboration draws upon the duo’s affinity for bold colors and familiar imagery, translating their graphic sensibilities into objects designed to accompany their owners throughout the day. The result is a collection that explores how artistic expression can become part of everyday life.

Across the collection, sticker-like illustrations, saturated hues, and expressive typography lend a sense of character to otherwise utilitarian surfaces. A collage of playful symbols evokes the spontaneity of a personal scrapbook, while the graphic “OK” design introduces a lighthearted note of optimism. Elsewhere, the cheerful “HI” motif transforms a magnetic wallet into a small, portable greeting. Each composition reflects Craig & Karl’s recognizable aesthetic while giving everyday accessories a more personal character.

It has been revealed that behind the playful graphics are the practical features that define ESR’s accessories. The Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Flex Stand incorporates a built-in adjustable stand, MagSafe compatibility, and protective construction, allowing it to move between different activities without sacrificing its colorful design. Coordinating magnetic wallets hold cards and cash in compact silhouettes, while the Magnetic Wallet Stand with Grip adds an adjustable viewing stand and finger loop for greater versatility. Together, these features bring Craig & Karl’s expressive graphics to everyday accessories.

The collection’s appeal also comes from the way it brings art into objects that have become nearly inseparable from modern life. Where traditional artworks invite observation, these designs encourage interaction, becoming more personal through repeated use. A phone placed on a café table, a wallet retrieved during a morning commute, or a device propped against a desk becomes a small, unexpected moment of visual interest.

Recent findings suggest that with Pocket Full of Joy, ESR and Craig & Karl make a case for bringing more creativity into the everyday. Sometimes, the most memorable design details are found in the things we carry without a second thought.

According to recent reports, the ESR × Craig & Karl Pocket Full of Joy collection will be available Nov. 14, 2026, at esr.com and amazon.com, with iPhone cases starting at $49.99 and magnetic wallets starting at $25.99.

Galloway extended the same material palette to these spaces, creating continuity throughout the property.

According to recent reports, rather than relying on dramatic gestures, Galloway lets the interplay of materials, textures, and forms define the interiors. It’s an approach that brings warmth and intimacy to a home of considerable scale.

The late Los Angeles artist Betye Saar receives heartfelt send-off at the Getty Center

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when a major artist dies, the tributes that come pouring in often gloss over personal shortcomings, whether the failure to complete educational degrees or the abandonment of wives and children.
  • Earlier this week the Getty filled its largest, 450-seat auditorium with fellow artists, curators, friends and family members of the artist, who died last July only four days short of her 100th birthday.
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the most powerful tributes came from her eldest nephew, Channing Johnson, who described her as a “true” if untraditional matriarch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when a major artist dies, the tributes that come pouring in often gloss over personal shortcomings, whether the failure to complete educational degrees or the abandonment of wives and children. But the memorial to Betye Saar this week at the Getty Center did just the opposite, setting into relief how powerfully she managed to balance—even integrate—acts of mothering and artmaking. (She also managed to earn her bachelor’s degree at the University of California, Los Angeles in 1949, a time when there were few Black students.).

Earlier this week the Getty filled its largest, 450-seat auditorium with fellow artists, curators, friends and family members of the artist, who died last July only four days short of her 100th birthday. The tone was sombre and celebratory, ending with her brother-in-law Bennie Maupin on saxophone and the band Bayou Bump leading a procession, as Saar had wanted.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most powerful tributes came from her eldest nephew, Channing Johnson, who described her as a “true” if untraditional matriarch. “She was as impactful and skilful as a family matriarch as she was a gifted artist. She gathered us together whether it was in a back yard or public park. She kept our family history in the forefront of our minds and in the public eye—you can literally see our family in her artwork,” he said, referring to assemblages where she incorporated family snapshots or memorabilia.

Johnson also celebrated Saar’s sense of humour and adventure, noting that she learned to belly dance early on and revealed off her dance moves in June when she was honoured by the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) at its Party in the Garden gala.

His tribute followed one by MoMA director Christophe Cherix, who recalled Saar’s studio in Laurel Canyon being “unlike any other studio I had ever seen…overflowing with treasures, almost archaeological, with objects patiently waiting sometimes years or even decades to be gathered, recognised [and] assembled into works of art”.

Betye Saar, Girl Children, 1964 © Betye Saar, courtesy of the artist and Roberts Projects, Los Angeles.

Sources indicate that saar’s longtime home and studio in Laurel Canyon is where she developed her deeply spiritualist, Black-centred, female-empowered vision through printmaking and assemblage, most famously using a windowpane to organise the esoteric, celestial images that make up the 1969 work Black Girl’s Window. It is also where she raised her three daughters: the sculptor Alison Saar, the mixed media artist Lezley Saar and the writer Tracye Saar. Early on they liked to pretend the wheel of their mother’s printing press was the helm of a pirate ship, and they have said in interviews they are happy they survived without losing a finger or hand.

The veteran Los Angeles collector Joy Simmons, who recalled bringing her week-old daughter Naima to a Saar opening at the Jan Baum gallery in 1981 (“I was not going to miss this opportunity to celebrate a Black woman opening up at a white woman’s gallery”), described the Saar creative lineage, which extends to grandchildren who work in the arts today.

Sources indicate that “To Alison, Lezley, Tracye and the whole family: I’ve watched three generations of Saar women make this city’s art history something special. Betye’s work belongs to museums now,” Simmons remarked, “but I know her proudest moment and her proudest accomplishment is all of you.”.

But look beyond the specifications, and you’ll find plenty of objects worth paying attention to: a clock that uses light and sound to mark the passing hours, a digital frame that resembles a printed photograph, and a cassette-playing boombox that brings back the pleasure of physical controls.

Sources indicate that for this year’s tech gift guide, we’ve selected 18 products that put as much thought into how they look and feel as what they do. Some embrace the past, others experiment with latest technology, and a few make the everyday business of charging, organizing, and staying connected a little more enjoyable.

Photography courtesy of MoMA Design Store.

Industry observers note that the boombox is back, complete with oversized speakers, analog controls, and illuminated VU meters. Dedicated physical controls make it easy to explore effects like double exposures, light painting, motion freeze, and split-shot compositions. It’s a refreshingly hands-on approach to photography that encourages a little spontaneity and plenty of happy accidents.

The Polaroid Mod Instant Camera is available at polaroid.com for $169.99.

To help manage body heat during workouts, the handheld device uses temperature-controlled surfaces to cool both palms simultaneously, with additional heat and contrast therapy settings. Compact and cordless, it provides an alternative to ice baths and other more cumbersome temperature-based recovery equipment.

Its carved aluminum body houses 75 LEDs that create an animated display, while built-in speakers play ambient soundscapes designed for focus, relaxation, and sleep. With customizable alarms, app connectivity, and USB-C charging, it’s a thoughtful alternative to the conventional bedside clock.

The Danish brand developed the H100 with replaceable components, including the ear cushions, headband, and batteries. The custom titanium drivers, soft leather detailing, and rich color options give them a distinctly luxurious feel, while advanced noise cancellation and immersive sound make the listening experience just as considered as the design. Chunky gray keys, red accents, and tactile mechanical switches establish the retro aesthetic, while an included joystick and two oversized programmable buttons bring arcade-style controls to the desktop. Bluetooth and wireless connectivity keep the throwback design compatible with contemporary setups.

The 8BitDo Retro Mechanical Keyboard N Edition is available at bestbuy.com for $79.99.

The Nest v2 is available at orbitkey.com for $125.

OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that what if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made?
  • Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.
  • “Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that what if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made? At Desa Potato Head in Bali, the new Good Times General Store explores that question through architecture, craftsmanship, and circular design. Created in collaboration with OMA, Potato Head’s first permanent retail space shifts the focus from consumption to discovery, inviting visitors to engage with the materials and processes behind the products.

Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.

“Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.

The architecture embraces a “contemporary-traditional” approach, bringing Balinese vernacular building techniques into a modern setting. An alang-alang thatch façade, made from locally sourced tropical grass, creates a textured outer layer, while rammed-earth walls made from local clay lend the interior a grounded, tactile quality. Bamboo appears throughout, including in the terrazzo flooring, where it’s used as an aggregate, and in the display elements.

“We wanted to reinterpret Balinese traditional architecture and craftsmanship in a contemporary way, rather than simply reproducing traditional forms or decorative elements,” says Ade Herkarisma, group head of architecture and development at Potato Head.

Reclaimed and locally sourced materials bring natural variations in color, texture, and form. Instead of concealing these irregularities, the designers embraced them, letting the materials guide the assembly and detailing.

Inside, the store unfolds across five interconnected bays, guiding visitors from finished products toward the processes behind their creation. The first showcases souvenirs and lifestyle objects by Indonesian craftspeople, while the second presents the Potato Head Collection, an apparel line inspired by Bali. The third introduces Wasted by Potato Head, a collaboration with British designer Max Lamb that transforms discarded materials into furniture and homewares.

Sources indicate that in the final two bays, visitors move from browsing to making. A working natural dye studio transforms food and plant waste into pigments used in workshops exploring dyeing, painting, and pattern-making. Beyond it, The Workshop features a wall of shredded HDPE plastic recovered from waste collectors across Bali and Java. The colorful fragments become part of the architecture, making the material’s previous life visible, while the surrounding space is dedicated to experimentation.

“While the first three bays focus on products and the stories behind them, the final two bays prioritize participation, inviting visitors to engage directly with materials and processes,” Gianotten explains.

Recent findings suggest that the store also connects to Desa Potato Head’s broader sustainability initiatives, including its Waste Lab and Follow the Waste Tour, which demonstrate how discarded materials can be recovered, processed, and transformed into upcoming objects. For OMA, the project extends ideas explored in N*thing is Possible, a 2022 exhibition in Singapore examining the potential of zero-waste hospitality.

“Circularity therefore becomes something experiential rather than abstract,” says Gianotten.

Designing around reclaimed resources required flexibility, especially around material consistency and availability. Rather than forcing materials into predetermined specifications, the team adapted the design to their natural characteristics and limitations.

Industry observers note that “We discovered that circularity goes beyond material selection,” Herkarisma explains. “It is about rethinking how we design, build, operate, and engage people in the process of giving newly introduced value to resources that would otherwise be discarded.”.

In a recent development, at the Good Times General Store, the act of making is as visible as the finished product. By placing workshops alongside retail displays and allowing reclaimed materials to shape the architecture, OMA and Potato Head offer a model of shopping that encourages visitors to look more closely at what they consume—and what might otherwise be thrown away.

Murrye Bernard is an architect-turned-writer covering architecture, interiors, product design, and sustainability. A registered architect, she has written for Architect, Architectural Record, Metropolis, Hospitality Design, Texas Architect, Green Building Advisor, and The Architect's Newspaper. She previously served as managing editor of Contract magazine and enjoys exploring the intersection of design, materials, and culture.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that this week, the newly-renamed ADAA Fair returns to the Park Avenue Armory (until 16 November), the first solely under the leadership of Kinsey Robb, who joined in 2024.
  • “It is still a small-scale collegial fair of the members, so that hasn't changed either.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that since 1989, the Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA) had hosted its Art Show, which brought member galleries from across the country together for an annual fair in New York. Last year, the ADAA cancelled the 2025 fair less than four months before it was set to open, citing a need to take a “strategic pause” to reevaluate how to best serve its members.

Recent findings suggest that this week, the newly-renamed ADAA Fair returns to the Park Avenue Armory (until 16 November), the first solely under the leadership of Kinsey Robb, who joined in 2024. Despite the fresh name and a few tweaks, it remains the same fair, she says.

“It’s a continuation. It's an evolution,” Robb says. “It is still a small-scale collegial fair of the members, so that hasn't changed either. It's just adapting into the environment and the time that we're in.”.

One of those new aspects is a smaller exhibitor list. This year, 63 galleries are participating, around 12 fewer than the last edition. The intention was to give the fair more focus in a time when dealers and collectors alike are complaining of "fairtigue", both due to frequency and size (Art Basel Miami Beach, the largest art fair in the Western Hemisphere, will also scale down participating galleries this year).

The hiatus “gave us an opportunity to look at the oversaturation of fairs that were happening at that time, and the fatigue that people were feeling,” Kinsey claims. “This scale feels nice to me.”.

In a recent development, the reduction allows for a larger space around the circular bar at the center of this year’s fair, affording attendees more space to move and cut through the three-aisle expo. Visitors naturally found themselves socialising at the centre of the fair during the opening gala for the Whitney Museum of American Art on Thursday (12 November), which was well-attended despite the stormy weather and even a tornado warning in New York City. (During the ADAA fair's hiatus, its longtime preview night partner and beneficiary, the Henry Street Settlement, teamed up with the Independent fair.).

The partnership with the Whitney Museum has brought in a latest, often-younger crowd, participating dealers say; works on display, meanwhile, skew heavily toward Modern and post-war secondary-market material rather contemporary works.

“I think deeply about the ecosystem of the art world, and how we all are connected,” Kinsey states. “Even if we all are in our own lanes or bubbles, we are all essential to each other in service of the art and in service of the artist.”.

The dealers participating range from stalwarts like Hirschl & Adler and Kraushaar Galleries, founding members of the ADAA who participated in the Art Show’s inaugural edition in 1989, to first-time exhibitors like Alexander Berggruen, Sargent's Daughters, Piero Atchugarry, Nicodim and Hollis Taggart.

Recent findings suggest that taggart has run his namesake gallery for nearly 50 years but only recently became an ADAA member, he states, allowing him to apply for and participate in the fair for the first time. He says that in the first few hours of the opening gala, he saw a great crowd of visitors, often from the surrounding Upper East Side, different from the crowd that comes to the openings in Chelsea, where he has a space. The gallery is presenting a dual stand dedicated to two women Abstract Expressionist painters: Michael (Corinne) West and Teruko Yokoi.

It has been revealed that “I think it's very mixed, it’s a bifurcated market,” Taggart says of the art market leading up to the fair. “There’s so many daily events that happen politically and financially, like the meltdown with Nvidia. I think the market's OK, but when you consider world events, it's a miracle that it's still as good as it is.”.

The most valuable transactions reported to date at the fair are Agnes Pelton’s The Well of Peace (1932), which had an asking price of $2.4m, and Beauford Delaney’s Untitled (Paris) (1986), which was priced at $1.6m, both from the stand of Newly introduced York-based dealer Jonathan Boos.

It has been revealed that another Upper East Side local, Kraushaar Galleries, reported the sale of two paintings for six-figure sums, as well as several works priced below $2,000. James Barron Art says it sold works by Beverly Pepper, Kenneth Noland and Kikuo Saito, each priced between $40,000 and $85,000, while Yoshii Gallery sold several works priced between $6,000 and $80,000. The Chelsea-based gallery and advisory firm AH Arts sold a work on paper by Helen Frankenthaler for $75,000. The international gallery Perrotin sold out of works by Susumu Kamijo, whose paintings on the stand were priced between $30,000 and 45,000. Jessica Silverman from San Francisco reported eight sales from its presentation of latest works by Julie Buffalohead, ranging in price from $22,000 and $50,000.

In a recent development, the Tribeca-based dealer Charles Moffett, who previously took part in the 2024 edition, says he appreciated the 2025 break and how the ADAA doesn’t pressure members to take part. During the opening gala, Moffett’s gallery sold four paintings by Lily Stockman priced at $20,000 apiece, and three paintings by Julia Jo priced at $30,000 each.

“With so many of the fairs, once you're on the hamster wheel, it's like, go go go. You apply every year, and if you don't apply or if you decide to sit out a year, you go to the back of the line,” Moffett says. “I'm just grateful that this feels more like an organisation that wants to see the best for each gallery.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City.
  • Titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date.
  • The slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City. Four monumental slides by artist Carsten Höller are the centerpiece of a major expansion at Antara, a mixed-use development designed by architecture firm Sordo Madaleno. The interactive installations bring an unexpected element of play to a destination that combines retail, hospitality, workplaces, and contemporary art.

Titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date. The four spiraling structures range from 39 to 125 feet in height, with lengths extending from approximately 102 to 295 feet. Rather than functioning as standalone sculptures, they are integrated into the architecture, connecting different parts of the development while giving visitors a fresh way to move between them.

The slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area. Their arrangement transforms what might otherwise be separate destinations into a shared experience, bringing people from different parts of the complex together in an unexpected way.

Sources indicate that “People sliding from a hotel, from offices, from restaurants, and from an art center are brought together in the air and land next to each other,” Höller explains. “They share the experience of being taken out of their usual form of being, into the unknown, dreamlike territory of simultaneous joy and fear.”.

The installation is part of the latest chapter for Antara, which opened in 2006 on a former industrial site in Mexico City’s Colonia Granada neighborhood. Developed by SOMA and designed by Sordo Madaleno, the original project introduced an open-air retail concept that has since evolved into a larger destination for shopping, dining, and cultural programming.

Recent findings suggest that twenty years later, the expansion places greater emphasis on the spaces between buildings and the ways visitors move through them. A latest 26,000-square-foot public garden, landscaped pathways, and stepped terraces connect the development’s different components, creating places to gather beyond its commercial spaces.

Art plays a central role in that approach. SOMA’s nonprofit contemporary art foundation, Arte Abierto, will open a fresh location within Antara, Arte Abierto Polanco, in December 2026. Alongside Höller’s installation, the venue will present Now What (2026), an exhibition by Danish artist collective Superflex that examines the relationship between built environments and natural forces. Combining architecture, sculpture, and text, the exhibition explores how human systems of design and organization influence our relationship with the surrounding world.

For SOMA president Javier Sordo Madaleno De Haro, the investment in publicly accessible space is fundamental to the development’s long-term value. “I’ve realized that the most valuable thing is not the capital gain of a building itself, but the value it brings to its surroundings,” he states. “Art and public space are how we create that value.”.

The expansion also introduces more than 80 latest retail brands and concepts, bringing Antara’s total to 260. A forthcoming 43-story tower will house Rosewood Mexico City, with 163 guest rooms and suites, restaurants, a spa, and an outdoor pool deck, along with office space for international companies.

In a recent development, yet the most distinctive addition may be the one that challenges how people typically navigate a building. By incorporating Höller’s slides directly into the architecture, Sordo Madaleno and SOMA have made art part of the development’s circulation, turning movement between spaces into an experience in its own right.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming public spaces and gardens are now open, while Mexico City Slides and the Superflex exhibition are scheduled to open in December. Access to the slides will be free, offering visitors a decidedly unconventional way to experience the evolving development.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, two typefaces carry the system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Studio Freight builds the Thesis brand identity from zine culture: an asterisk mark, dot-grid Harber type, and electric lime.

Industry observers note that the system starts from a position, not a logo. Thesis builds brands on Bitcoin, backing its conviction with capital and code, and Studio Freight answers with a visual language pulled from indie hacker zines and early computing: black and white, gritty textures, hand-drawn spheres and gears, and one electric lime doing all the shouting. The asterisk sits at the center, somewhere between a footnote and a flag, and the whole identity reads like a samizdat pamphlet that learned to behave on a screen. The voice matches, what the studio calls adult punk: spirited defiance tempered with wisdom, unafraid to make guesses about restoring autonomy in tech.

According to recent reports, two typefaces carry the system. Harber, a dot-gridded display face, holds the texture of a printout from a different internet, with dotted letterforms that spell the name at poster scale, in the site navigation, and ghosted behind the asterisk on the homepage. Antique Legacy Semibold does the clear work, setting plain statements in a voice that stays readable while the display type makes the noise.

The grid is the dot grid itself. The asterisk mark, the dotted THESIS letterforms, and the dotted figures in the launch graphics all sit on the same dotted construction, so every panel reads as one argument. The studio coined a word for the position behind it, counterventure, naming a studio that creates ideas from the inside instead of waiting for them to walk in, operating against the extractive defaults of the venture model.

Sources indicate that the material language is print, even on screen. Hand-drawn spheres and gears, gritty textures, and a black-and-white field give the system the feel of print passed hand to hand, and the electric lime cuts through it in exactly one place at a time: a poster, a headline, a hand-drawn illustration on a lime field. The stationery keeps the same discipline, a white card that carries the name and the counterventure label, and nothing else.

The system stretches across the launch site, where the asterisk fills a monitor above the tagline, and into product work, where a phone screen for tBTC carries the dot-grid mark and a line about decentralized cryptography. A poster fills its frame with one word in flat lime, and a manifesto sheet sets the studio's own words in typewriter type over the dotted asterisk, including its line about making bitcoin accessible to all.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co.
  • Discovered in Arkansas in 1926, the 27.21-carat Arkansas Diamond was acquired by Tiffany & Co.
  • In a recent development, the Arkansas Diamond is displayed alongside archival documents tracing the state’s diamond-mining history in Nature Adorned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co. ultimately acquired and dubbed the Arkansas Diamond. One hundred years later, that pretty rock has returned to its home state as a highlight of Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

Discovered in Arkansas in 1926, the 27.21-carat Arkansas Diamond was acquired by Tiffany & Co. in 1946 and is among the largest diamonds ever found in the United States. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

In a recent development, the Arkansas Diamond is displayed alongside archival documents tracing the state’s diamond-mining history in Nature Adorned. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

The diamond’s acquisition reflects a longstanding Tiffany tradition. Under the leadership of George Frederick Kunz, the organization’s first chief gemologist, Tiffany championed American gemstones at a time when European jewelers largely overlooked them. From sapphires sourced in Montana and tourmalines from Maine to emeralds from North Carolina, these stones reveal the geological diversity of the American landscape. The Arkansas Diamond is another example of that legacy.

An 1885–1895 Tiffany & Co. necklace features 30 multicolored American-mined tourmalines, a gemstone championed by the organization’s first chief gemologist, George Frederick Kunz. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Sources indicate that A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Bringing together gemstones and jewelry from The Tiffany Archives with works from the museum’s collection, Nature Adorned explores how the natural world has influenced both jewelry and fine art. Through unexpected pairings, the exhibition reveals shared approaches to color, form, and craftsmanship across different mediums.

It has been revealed that installation view of Nature Adorned at Crystal Bridges, where gemstones, jewelry, and works of American art are presented in conversation with one another. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Recent findings suggest that “This exhibition reveals the power of seeing The Tiffany Archives and Crystal Bridges’ collection in conversation,” notes Jen Padgett, Crystal Bridges’ Windgate curator of craft. “Through this collaboration, we can highlight the remarkable creativity, attention to materials, and skilled making that have shaped American art and design across generations.”.

Sources indicate that inside the exhibition, this conversation begins in the garden. George Paulding Farnham’s orchid brooches balance the fluidity of the natural world with the precision of cut gemstones. Diamonds, emeralds, and pink sapphires are delicately placed among gold and enamel, capturing the flowers with botanical accuracy.

George Paulding Farnham’s Tiger Orchid brooch (1889–1893) combines gold, sterling silver, diamonds, emeralds, pink sapphires, and enamel to capture the flower’s intricate details. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Industry observers note that martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle (ca. 1875–1890) reflects the same fascination with botanical detail found in Farnham’s orchid jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

The brooches reflect the paintings displayed alongside them, including Martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle. The paintings share the same attention to organic form and detail, making the two distinct works feel like an extensions of one another—and of nature itself.

George Paulding Farnham’s orchid-inspired jewelry is displayed alongside works of American art in Nature Adorned, highlighting a shared interest in the natural world’s intricate forms. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean (1965) and Leon Polk Smith’s Upcoming Moon for August (1983) introduce a different interpretation of nature, where form is reduced to crisp edges and angles. The exhibition pairs these abstract works with faceted gemstones, drawing attention to the relationship between shape, line, and geometry.

In a recent development, A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

While Herrera and Polk Smith focus on precision, Jean Schlumberger lets loose. His rubellite and turquoise necklace, Hedges and Flowers, along with his tanzanite brooch, Bird on a Rock, capture what he described as the “irregularity of the universe.” Instead of taming nature, Schlumberger allows its unpredictability to take the spotlight. Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately echoes this organic approach through lively colors and patterns, creating a visual dialogue with the jewels.

Jean Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace (1978–1987) combines gold, platinum, diamonds, rubellite tourmalines, and turquoise in an exuberant interpretation of the natural world. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace on display at Crystal Bridges, where its organic forms are presented in dialogue with works of American art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Victoria Reynolds, Tiffany & Co.’s chief gemologist and vice president of high jewelry diamond and gemstone acquisition, describes the exhibition as a celebration of the company’s heritage, highlighting “the enduring influence of nature across generations of creativity.”.

Jean Schlumberger’s Bird on a Rock brooch (1965) pairs a diamond-studded bird with a striking tanzanite gemstone, transforming a familiar natural subject into an imaginative piece of jewelry. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

According to recent reports, hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately (2011) uses expressive color and pattern to explore organic forms, echoing the playful approach to nature found in Jean Schlumberger’s jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination is on view through Mar. 29, 2027, at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

How Klafs Is Rethinking the Sauna Through Design

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the sauna is Finnish.
  • It has been revealed that at Klafs headquarters, where the organization’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a two-tiered, glass-enclosed sauna.
  • Sources indicate that in German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” In a wellness context, it refers to a guided sauna ritual, typically involving water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the sauna is Finnish. The company reimagining it for contemporary homes and spas is German. Klafs, based in Schwäbisch Hall, Germany, sees no contradiction. Its designers approach the centuries-old ritual through engineering, experimenting with heat, air, and materials. As wellness culture expands, the language surrounding its rituals has become increasingly fluid. In my own friend group, “banya” has become nearly shorthand for any spa visit, though it refers specifically to the Russian-style bathhouse. Klafs, by contrast, brings a distinctly German engineering sensibility to these traditions, asking how far the experience can be pushed.

It has been revealed that at Klafs headquarters, where the organization’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a two-tiered, glass-enclosed sauna. Our guide, an experienced training manager named Heinrich, speaks to the heater in the corner. “Hey, Klafs,” he states, with the intonation we’ve learned from Alexa and other voice-activated devices. I hadn’t considered the possibility of a smart aufguss guide.

Sources indicate that in German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” In a wellness context, it refers to a guided sauna ritual, typically involving water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air. The practice has helped make sauna-going a communal experience in many North American spas. Klafs’s Vitality Boost, which the tech giant describes as the world’s first personalized heat-waving system, brings elements of that ritual into an automated setting: no towel-spinning guide required, and no need to leave the wooden bench.

According to recent reports, blue lighting, textured surfaces, and a sculptural ice fountain transform Klafs’s Frimas ice steam room into an immersive cooling environment. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

From the heat of the sauna, the tour moves into an altogether different climate. I retreat into the cool blue light of a Frimas ice steam room, where a glowing central ice fountain grows delicate, flower-like formations.

Recent findings suggest that around the corner, a button labeled “snow” summons flurries from the ceiling of the ice steam shower. The cooling phase of a hot-and-cold bathing ritual isn’t where most people want to linger, but these spaces make a compelling case for slowing down. Rather than treating cold exposure as something to endure, KLAFS creates immersive environments that make it part of the experience.

Sources indicate that klafs brings the experience of winter indoors with a snow room featuring ice-covered surfaces, dramatic lighting, and a rocky landscape. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Then there’s the foam. I also discovered foam steam baths, which replace the intensity of a traditional aufguss with a more playful, tactile experience. Steam rooms equipped for foam treatments can be integrated into hotel and spa programming as scheduled group experiences. The suds, reminiscent of childhood bubble baths and the elaborate foam sculptures they inspired, bring out a part of my inner child I had long since stowed away. Espuro, Klafs’s proprietary foam essence, is formulated with plant-based ingredients, including coconut-derived compounds, which the manufacturer says help care for skin exposed to heat.

Sources indicate that designed in collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, Klafs’s S11 sauna incorporates horizontal wood slats and integrated lighting into a contemporary residential interior. Photographycourtesy of Klafs.

Beyond these sensory experiments, Klafs has also reconsidered the sauna itself as an architectural object. The retractable S1 sauna expands from a compact enclosure into a full-size sauna, addressing the spatial constraints that often keep one out of the home. The design-led S11, a collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, pairs delicate washi paper and multicolor light panels with smooth, sinuous lines.

Inside the S11, continuous horizontal slats, curved corners, and concealed lighting create a sculptural interior that emphasizes materiality and form. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Long established in Germany, Klafs has been expanding into the American market since its acquisition by Kohler in 2024. The premium Altea fitness club in my city, for instance, features Klafs installations, including the Sanarium and Polaris Ice Room. Yet what stays with me after the visit isn’t a particular product. It’s the willingness to question what a sauna, steam room, or cooling space can be. At Klafs, even the most familiar wellness rituals seem open to reinvention.

Warm wood surfaces, tiered seating, and integrated lighting define a Klafs sauna at Hotel Sonne-Post, a spa hotel in Waldau, Germany. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Latest Update: Lotus L. Kang wins Canada’s top art prize, the Sobey Art Award

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the National Gallery of Canada (NGC) and the Sobey Art Foundation named the artist Lotus L.
  • The other five shortlisted artists—Melaw Nakehk'o (from the Circumpolar region), Samuel Roy-Bois (Pacific), Audie Murray (Prairies), Caroline Monnet (Québec) and Shane Perley-Dutcher (Atlantic)—will each receive C$25,000 ($17,500), while the 24 longlisted artists each received C$10,000 ($7,000), bringing the total value of the award to C$465,000 ($325,800).
  • It has been revealed that in a statement, Jonathan Shaughnessy, the chair of the jury for this year’s Sobey Art Award, praised Kang for “the commitment and rigour demonstrated in her practice for well over a decade”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the National Gallery of Canada (NGC) and the Sobey Art Foundation named the artist Lotus L. Kang asthe winner of the 2026 Sobey Art Award during a ceremony on Saturday (14 November). The Toronto-born, New York-based photographer, sculptor and installation artist won the 23rd edition of the annual award, the most high-profile and lucrative prize devoted to Canadian contemporary artists, and will receive C$100,000 ($70,000).

The other five shortlisted artists—Melaw Nakehk'o (from the Circumpolar region), Samuel Roy-Bois (Pacific), Audie Murray (Prairies), Caroline Monnet (Québec) and Shane Perley-Dutcher (Atlantic)—will each receive C$25,000 ($17,500), while the 24 longlisted artists each received C$10,000 ($7,000), bringing the total value of the award to C$465,000 ($325,800).

It has been revealed that in a statement, Jonathan Shaughnessy, the chair of the jury for this year’s Sobey Art Award, praised Kang for “the commitment and rigour demonstrated in her practice for well over a decade”. He continued: “Through installations using unfixed photographic film, cast and found objects, and fabricated armatures, her practice resists the stabilising impulses traditionally associated with photography. Reoccurring motifs including lotus root, flowers, soju bottles, birds, anchovies, are not fixed objects, but repositories of place, longing and desire.”.

Recent findings suggest that partial view of Lotus L. Kang's installation In Cascades (2023-24) in Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing at the Whitney Museum of American Art Photo: The Art Newspaper.

Recent findings suggest that kang, a recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2024 whose work was included in the 2024 Whitney Biennial and the 2025 Shanghai Biennale, works across sculpture, photography and site-responsive installation. Her materially dense, non-linear installations explore the liminal space between industrial and architectural forms, familial and social histories, as well as poetry and non-human figures. One of her celebrated installation works, Mother (2020), comprised dozens of metal mixing bowls filled with scattered abstract clay, rubber and stone sculptures as well as aluminium casts of fruit and anchovies. Her critically acclaimed solo exhibition at 52 Walker in New York last year featured several greenhouse installations as well as one made of strips of film extended around a spinning rotary dryer.

“It is an honour to be recognised by this prize,” Kang said in a statement. “I am grateful to those I love, those who love me and those who have supported me; you keep me going. The recognition of this prize means that askew ideas are worth pursuing. Art is essential to life, progress and love.”.

During the ceremony, Kang told those assembled at the NGC and those watching via livestream: “I just want to congratulate the other artists. It’s an honour to be nominated alongside you. Shane, Melaw, Caroline, Audie, Samuel. It is really inspiring to be showing alongside you, and who knows what would have happened, and I’m just glad we’ll all keep making art, because it’s really the best thing. So, thank you so much.’’.

Lotus L. Kang, Receiver Transmitter (49 Echoes I), 2022-25 © Lotus Kang. Photo: Courtesy of the artist and 52 Walker gallery, Fresh York.

According to recent reports, rob Sobey, the chair of the Sobey Art Foundation, offered his “heartfelt congratulations” to Kang and added: “We also celebrate tonight all 29 artists on this year’s longlist and shortlist for their creativity and vision. We are proud to champion their work and grateful to the National Gallery of Canada for helping bring these remarkable artistic voices to audiences at home and around the world.”.

Selected by an independent jury of curators and cultural leaders, Kang was chosen following a rigorous review process. The jury, who evaluated the artists’ practices, achievements, and contributions to contemporary art in Canada included Kimberly Phillips, the director of the Marianne and Edward Gibson Art Museum at Simon Fraser University, representing the Pacific region;Daisy Desrosiers, a curator at large for North America at Tate, representing the Quebec region;and Helen Nisbet, the director of Glasgow International, serving as international juror.

Works by all six shortlisted artists are currently featured in the 2026 Sobey Art Award Exhibition at the NGC in Ottawa (until 3 January 2027).

The late Frank H. Sobey, an enthusiastic collector of Canadian art, established the Sobey Art Foundation in 1981 and the Sobey Art Award was launched in 2002. Five years ago, the award’s criteria were amended from a prize devoted to “emerging artists” under 40 to recognising artists of any age who are at a “critical juncture” in their careers. Past winners have included Brian Jungen (in 2002), Annie Pootoogook (2006), Abbas Akhavan (2015), Laakkuluk Williamson Bathory (2021) and Nico Williams (2024).
